en.tldr: `Read(...)` and `Edit(...)` rules use gitignore patterns with four anchors, and choosing the wrong anchor silently points the rule at another directory. `WebFetch(domain:...)` gates fetches by hostname. Use them to fence which files and domains Claude's tools may touch.
whenToUse: Blocking Claude from reading secrets such as `.env` files
Protecting a directory from edits for the whole team
Writing a user-level rule that must apply in every project
Allowing web fetches only to specific domains
keyFacts: `//path` is absolute from the filesystem root; `~/path` is from your home directory.
`/path` is relative to the settings source: the primary working directory for project and local settings, `~/.claude` for user settings.
`path` or `./path` is relative to the current directory; a bare filename like `Read(.env)` matches at any depth under it.
Write file rules as `Edit(...)`: `Write`, `NotebookEdit` and `MultiEdit` path rules are accepted but never consulted, with a startup warning.
A `Read` deny also blocks the Edit and Write tools on the same path.
`WebFetch(domain:example.com)` matches by hostname; `*.example.com` matches subdomains but not `example.com` itself.
gotchas: `/Users/alice/file` isn't absolute in a rule; use `//Users/alice/file`.
`Read(/secrets/**)` in user settings blocks `~/.claude/secrets/**`, not a project's `secrets` directory.
Read and Edit deny rules don't stop a script that opens files itself or `grep -r` without naming the file; use the sandbox for OS-level blocking.
NotebookEdit isn't covered by a `Read` deny; add an `Edit` deny for paths no tool may change.

confusedWith.difference: In `sandbox.filesystem` arrays `/path` is absolute; in Read/Edit rules you need `//path`.
Bash rules match command text with `*`; Read/Edit rules match file paths with gitignore patterns.

questions.stem: A team wants to stop Claude from modifying anything in the `migrations/` directory at the project root. The rule must be shared with everyone who clones the repo. Which deny rule and location should they use?

options.why: In project settings `/path` anchors at the primary working directory, and `Edit` rules apply to all built-in editing tools.
Path rules for `Write` are accepted but never consulted; file permissions check only `Edit` and `Read`.
`//` anchors at the filesystem root, so it targets `/migrations`, not the project directory.
In user settings `/path` resolves under `~/.claude`, and user settings aren't shared.

questions.explanation: File modification rules must use `Edit`, which applies to all built-in tools that edit files; `Write` path rules are never consulted. A single leading slash anchors at the settings source, which is the primary working directory for `.claude/settings.json`. The double slash would point at the filesystem root instead. User settings would anchor at `~/.claude` and wouldn't reach teammates.
keywordCues: shared with everyone who clones the repo

es.stem: Un equipo quiere impedir que Claude modifique cualquier cosa del directorio `migrations/` en la raíz del proyecto. La regla debe compartirse con todos los que clonen el repo. ¿Qué regla deny y qué ubicación deben usar?

`//` ancla en la raíz del sistema de archivos, así que apunta a `/migrations`, no al proyecto.
En settings de usuario `/ruta` se resuelve bajo `~/.claude`, y esos settings no se comparten.

es.explanation: Las reglas de modificación de archivos deben usar `Edit`, que aplica a todas las herramientas que editan archivos; las reglas de ruta con `Write` nunca se consultan. Una sola barra inicial ancla en el origen del settings, que para `.claude/settings.json` es el directorio de trabajo principal. La doble barra apuntaría a la raíz del sistema de archivos. Los settings de usuario anclarían en `~/.claude` y no llegarían al equipo.

options.why: In user settings a single `/` anchors at `~/.claude`, so this targets `~/.claude/code`.
`~/` anchors at the home directory, so the rule covers every repository under `~/code` from user settings.
An `Edit` deny blocks changes, not reads; a `Read` deny is what blocks reading.
`./` is relative to the current directory, which changes with each session.

questions.explanation: To write a user-settings rule that applies inside every project, the docs say to use a `//` absolute path or a `~/` home-relative path. A single leading slash in user settings resolves under `~/.claude`, which is the trap. A `./` pattern depends on the session's current directory. Reading is blocked by a `Read` deny, not an `Edit` deny.

es.stem: Un desarrollador guarda todos sus repositorios bajo `~/code`. Desde un solo lugar, sin tocar cada proyecto, quiere impedir que Claude lea cualquier `.env` en todos esos repositorios. ¿Qué regla deny debe agregar a `~/.claude/settings.json`?

Un deny de `Edit` bloquea cambios, no lecturas; lo que bloquea leer es un deny de `Read`.
`./` es relativo al directorio actual, que cambia en cada sesión.

es.explanation: Para que una regla en settings de usuario aplique dentro de cada proyecto, la documentación indica usar una ruta absoluta con `//` o una relativa al home con `~/`. Una sola barra inicial en settings de usuario se resuelve bajo `~/.claude`, y esa es la trampa. Un patrón con `./` depende del directorio actual de la sesión. questions.stem: A project denies `Read(./.env)` and Claude runs from the directory that holds `.env`. The team wants to know which access paths remain open and would still need the sandbox to block. Which two actions are NOT stopped by the rule? (Choose two.)

options.text: Claude runs a Python script that opens `.env` itself.
options.why: Read deny rules don't apply to subprocesses that read files indirectly.
`cat` is a file command Claude Code recognizes in Bash, so the Read deny applies.

options.text: Claude uses the Edit tool on `.env`.
options.why: A `Read` deny also blocks the Edit and Write tools on the same path.
A command that reads files without naming them isn't covered by the deny rule.

options.text: Claude uses the Read tool on `.env`.
options.why: This is exactly what a Read deny rule blocks.

questions.explanation: Read and Edit deny rules apply to Claude's built-in file tools and to file commands Claude Code recognizes in Bash, such as `cat`. A `Read` deny also blocks the Edit and Write tools on the same path. They don't apply to commands that read files without naming them, like `grep -r pattern .`, or to scripts that open files themselves. For OS-level blocking of every process, enable the sandbox.

es.stem: Un proyecto tiene deny `Read(./.env)` y Claude corre desde el directorio que contiene `.env`. El equipo quiere saber qué vías de acceso quedan abiertas y todavía necesitarían el sandbox. ¿Qué dos acciones NO frena la regla? (Elige dos.)

es.explanation: Los deny de Read y Edit aplican a las herramientas de archivos de Claude y a comandos de archivos que Claude Code reconoce en Bash, como `cat`. Un deny de `Read` también bloquea Edit y Write en esa ruta. No aplican a comandos que leen archivos sin nombrarlos, como `grep -r pattern .`, ni a scripts que abren archivos por su cuenta. Para bloquear a todo proceso a nivel de sistema operativo, activa el sandbox.

questions.stem: Write the deny rule that blocks reading any `.env` file anywhere on the filesystem.
questions.explanation: `//` anchors the pattern at the filesystem root and `**` matches across directories, so `Read(//**/.env)` blocks every `.env` anywhere. A plain `Read(.env)` only covers `.env` files at or under the current directory.
keywordCues: any `.env` file anywhere on the filesystem

es.stem: Escribe la regla deny que bloquea leer cualquier archivo `.env` en cualquier parte del sistema de archivos.
es.explanation: `//` ancla el patrón en la raíz del sistema de archivos y `**` cruza directorios, así que `Read(//**/.env)` bloquea todo `.env` en cualquier lugar. Un `Read(.env)` simple solo cubre los `.env` en el directorio actual o debajo.

recall.prompt: You copy `/etc/secrets/**` from a sandbox filesystem setting into a `Read(...)` deny rule. Why doesn't it block the absolute path?
recall.promptEs: Copias `/etc/secrets/**` de una configuración de filesystem del sandbox a un deny `Read(...)`. ¿Por qué no bloquea la ruta absoluta?
recall.idealAnswer: In sandbox filesystem paths a leading `/` is absolute, but in Read and Edit rules a single `/` anchors at the settings source, such as the project directory. To target the absolute path in a permission rule you must write `Read(//etc/secrets/**)`.
rubric: Permission rules treat /path as relative to the settings source
